Thank you for submitting your article "Unimodal statistical learning produces multimodal object-like representations" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers including the Reviewing Editor, and the evaluation has been overseen by Michael Frank as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Michael Landy (Reviewer #1); Samuel J Gershman (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

The paper "Unimodal statistical learning produces multimodal object-like representations" presents an elegant series of two experiments, demonstrating that human adults can make cross-modal inferences without bimodal training. Participants learned either haptically or visually that two particular shapes tend to form an object. In the visual condition the critical cue was the probability of the co-occurrence of the two shapes, in the haptic condition the force necessary to pull them apart. The authors show that these learned regularities generalize to a test in the other domain. Overall, we found the paper clearly written, interesting, and insightful.

1) While all reviewers agreed that the experiments provided new interesting insights in the learning and cross-modal generalization of learning, the theoretical link to the formation of objects is not as well motivated and may require a more careful treatment (see major comment from Sam Gershman and Jörn Diedrichsen). Specifically, the extant literature on the principles of object perception clearly provides evidence that boundary cues are important in the formation of objects (Spelke, 1990, etc.). While the authors show that statistical regularities can be learned and generalized across modalities, the paper does not provide any insight into the importance of boundary cues vs. statistical regularities. This should be better reflected in paper.

2) Yildirim and Jacobs, 2012, 2013, 2015; see also Erdogan, Yildirim and Jacobs, 2015, have developed computational models and provided empirical evidence for modality-independent representations of objects. This literature should be cited and the current work placed better in this context.

3) The reviewers and the reviewing editor were not 100% convinced by the argument that conscious awareness did not drive the learning/generalization effects. The authors do not even report the average score on the explicit test. What would help is to present data on explicit knowledge and generalization as a scatter plot. If all subjects showed high levels of performance on the explicit task, the validity of the partial correlation approach would be seriously called into question.

I am appending the original 3 reviews below for more details.

Reviewing Editor:

The paper "Unimodal statistical learning produces multimodal object-like representations" presents two elegant experiments, in which participants either haptically or visually learn that two particular shapes tend to form an object. In the visual condition the critical cue was the probability of the co-occurrence of the two shapes, in the haptic condition the force necessary to pull them apart. The authors show that these learned regularities then generalized to a test in the other domain.

Overall, I found the paper clearly written, interesting and insightful. I believe there are overall some weaknesses in the presentation of the results, and particularly in the strength of some of the statistical results (i.e. there is really no real evidence for a haptic -> visual generalization at the group level).

Furthermore, the motivation for the study is based a lot on how objects are learned in childhood. This arises two critical questions: Do the authors believe that the learning rules uncovered from an experiment in adults has anything to do with how 4-month old start to understand the world. Secondly, "objectness" is probably learned to a large degree by visual or haptic (as in surface touch) boundaries. Showing that adults CAN learn statistical regularities does not show that this is indeed the driving mechanism behind the acquisition of objects. Indeed, one might argue that statistical co-occurrence is not enough. For example, I often wear pants, but that doesn't make them and me one object?

Reviewer #1:

OK, this isn't typical reviewer-speak: This paper is really fun! It's such a good example of true synergistic collaboration, since it so obviously combines the diverse threads of the authors' previous work. And the result is a cool paradigm and a convincing set of data. I really don't have much in the way of useful comments, which is not typical for me. (OK, my comments might not usually be useful, but at least there are usually a lot of comments; ^) And that you managed to work in one of your chimera namesakes… Really, these are very well-designed, careful experiments. I wonder if the "objecthood" led observers to perceive, fuzzy as they might have been, something in the way of illusory contours between objects, especially since the location of these contours was cued in the haptic pulling training in the second experiment.

Subsection “Visual statistical exposure”: Here I did my usual OCD check on the methods and couldn't come up with 444 as the number of distinct possible stimuli. By my count, there are 8 each configurations with 3 horizontal or 3 vertical pair placements, and assuming you place the pairs without replacement, that's 2x8x6 = 96 stimuli. And, there are 14 configurations each with either 2 horizontal and 1 vertical or vice versa, yielding 2x14x(3x2x3) = 504 stimuli, for a total of 600. I'm not sure where I went wrong or how you got 444.

Subsection “Visual familiarity test”: I also checked the arithmetic here. It works, but it assumes that the pseudopairs take a left-side pattern from one true pair and combine it with a right-side pattern from another true pair, and keep them on their former sides. That's a good choice for keeping the pseudopair statistics similar to the true pair statistics, but you don't state explicitly that that's what you did.

Subsection “Haptic statistical exposure”, last paragraph: There are fewer scenes to learn in this experiment than in the visual training experiment and they were visible for much more time (not restricted to 700 ms).

Supplementary Figure 3: I'm glad this figure was included, although I'd put it in the main text. It's worthwhile seeing how much the pulling forces were modulated relative to the correct values. You might even cite this as a learning "gain" proportion (about 20%, to my eye).

Reviewer #2:

This paper presents an elegant series of experiments of visual-haptic integration, demonstrating that human adults can make cross-modal inferences without bimodal training. The authors argue that these results support theories of object perception based on learned statistical regularities. The paper is well-written and thorough. My main concerns are about conceptual foundations and novelty.

The definition of an object as "a material thing that can be seen and touched" is too weak, because it does not adhere to the constraints evident in infant (and adult) object cognition (as an aside, it's rather odd to use a dictionary definition when so much ink has been spilled on this question in cognitive science). Spelke, 1990, defines physical objects as "persisting bodies with internal unity and stable boundaries" (p. 30). She presents evidence that infant object perception adheres to four constraints: cohesion, boundedness, rigidity, and no action at a distance. It's important to note that a material thing can have statistical regularities without satisfying any of these constraints. For example, consider the jet of steam spouting from a boiling teapot. It's a material thing with statistical regularities (following gas laws, thermodynamics, etc.); it can be seen and touched. But it is not cohesive, bounded, or rigid. The experiments of Kellman and Spelke, 1983, and many others, show that the same arrangement of visible surfaces can be perceived as an object or not, depending on whether it adheres to these constraints.

To continue this point, the conceptual issue here is that the authors consider objects to be bundles of statistical regularities that support inferences about hidden properties: "participants should be able to predict haptic properties of objects based on just visual statistics, without any prior haptic experience with them, and vice versa, predict visual properties based on haptic statistical exposure alone." No doubt observed statistical regularities do support such inferences (this is what Spelke refers to as the "empiricist" account, which she criticizes). But the key insight from Spelke and others is that object perception goes beyond observed statistical regularities. There are inductive constraints on objecthood that support stronger generalizations. This conceptual issue could be resolved if the authors step back from their strong claims about the nature of objecthood, and instead focus on more restricted claims about how statistical learning shapes multimodal generalization.

I was surprised that the authors don't cite the work of Yildirim and Jacobs, 2012, 2013, 2015; see also Erdogan, Yildirim and Jacobs, 2015, which seems highly relevant. In fact, I feel that these prior papers diminish the novelty of the present paper, since Yildirim and colleagues showed empirical evidence for modality-independent representations of objects, and moreover they developed sophisticated computational models of how these representations are acquired and used.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Unimodal statistical learning produces multimodal object-like representations" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by a Reviewing Editor and Michael Frank as the Senior Editor.

The manuscript has been improved to address most of the remaining issues. However, before final acceptance, I would like to request a couple of clarifications on the explicit awareness task to be presented in the paper (Materials and methods, and Figure 4 legend):

You say that "Participants were asked whether they noticed that the shapes came in pairs and if so then the shapes were presented to them individually and they had to point to the shapes that they thought were part of the inventory."

Does this mean that some of the participants were not presented with the objects if they said they didn't know? If yes, how many participants? Was their performance labeled with 0?

The information in the caption seems to indicate that "explicitness" is the proportion of correctly identified pairs out of 6+4 =10 possible pairs. Why are the proportion correct not in {0, 0.1, 0.2.…, 1}?

I assume the test was conducted by placing 12 (or 8) objects on the table and let the participants pick out candidate pairs (although the Materials and methods state that you showed the objects individually). Please clarify. Also, please indicate whether you asked the participants to "guess" remaining pairs or did you let them stop when they did not feel they knew?

If you forced participants to guess, please indicate chance performance on your explicit memory test.

If the participants were not forced to guess remaining pairs, please state this clearly. Given the standards in the memory literature, a force-choice test is the most stringent way to assess the presence/absence of explicit memory. Subjects may say they do not "know", but still be able to "guess" very much above chance. Without a forced-choice assessment, one is testing mostly meta-memory, but not explicit memory. So if this is the approach you took, I think the limitations of the explicit test should be pointed out in the Discussion.

results.result: The experimental design successfully created artificial objects defined solely by statistical contingencies without informative boundary cues. Objects were defined as unique pairs of unfamiliar shapes, with only individual shapes having visible boundaries. The separation between shapes was uniform regardless of whether they belonged to the same or different objects, making boundary cues uninformative for object identification.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C113 collectively describe a well-controlled experimental design where objects are defined purely by statistical co-occurrence rather than visual boundaries. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate controls (uniform spacing, no color differences, no explicit instructions about objects), and the design directly addresses the research question about statistical learning without boundary cues.

results.result: After visual exposure to scenes containing true pairs, participants performed significantly above chance (77% correct, 95% CI: 0.67-0.87, p=1.9×10⁻⁵, Bayes factor=1253) in judging true pairs as more familiar than pseudo pairs, despite equal exposure to all constituent shapes.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 report strong within-modality visual learning with robust statistical support (large effect size, highly significant p-value, strong Bayes factor). The finding replicates previous work (Fiser & Aslin 2001, 2005) and demonstrates that participants learned the statistical structure of the visual scenes.

results.result: Visual statistical learning generalized to haptic judgments: participants performed significantly above chance (ρ=0.27, 95% CI: 0.07-0.47, p=0.0095, Bayes factor=5) in predicting pulling forces for novel objects without any haptic experience. The correlation between visual and haptic performance covered 87% of the possible performance range, with no significant learning trend during testing (p=0.07), suggesting immediate generalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C33 demonstrate cross-modal generalization from visual to haptic domain. While the average effect is modest (Bayes factor=5), the correlation analysis and lack of learning during testing support genuine zero-shot generalization. The statistical model fit (87% coverage) provides quantitative evidence for the relationship between visual learning and haptic performance.

results.result: After haptic exposure, participants performed significantly above chance in the haptic pulling test (ρ=0.28, 95% CI: 0.14-0.42, p=3.8×10⁻³, Bayes factor=91) and generalized to visual familiarity judgments (60% correct, 95% CI: 0.51-0.69, p=0.038, Bayes factor=2). True pairs were judged more visually familiar despite identical visual statistics, with the effect appearing immediately without gradual learning (p=0.58).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C47 demonstrate bidirectional cross-modal transfer. The haptic learning is well-supported (strong Bayes factor=91), though the visual generalization is weaker (Bayes factor=2) as expected given the explicit conflict between visual and haptic statistics in this experiment. The immediate appearance of effects supports genuine generalization rather than learning during testing.

results.result: Comparison across experiments revealed similar haptic performance levels (t(18)=0.09, p=0.93, Bayes factor=3) despite the first experiment having no haptic exposure. Visual familiarity performance was higher after visual exposure than haptic exposure (t(18)=2.65, p=0.01, Bayes factor=4), consistent with the different cue conflict structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 provide important cross-experiment comparisons. The similar haptic performance despite different exposure conditions (C48-C49) strengthens the generalization argument. The difference in visual performance (C50-C51) is appropriately explained by the experimental design differences (cue conflict in haptic exposure experiment).

results.result: Within-participant analysis revealed significantly positive consistency (correlation=0.297±0.104, t(34)=2.86, p=0.007, Bayes factor=6) between which pairs participants treated as objects in visual familiarity versus haptic pulling tests, demonstrating modality-generic object representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 provide critical evidence that the cross-modal effects reflect unified object representations rather than generic attention effects. The within-participant consistency analysis is methodologically sound and the statistical support is adequate (Bayes factor=6), though the effect is modest in magnitude.

results.result: Visual and haptic performance strongly correlated across participants (R=0.84, p=6.2×10⁻⁷, Bayes factor=3225). When controlling for explicit knowledge of pairs, a highly significant partial correlation remained (R=0.69, p=3.1×10⁻⁴, Bayes factor=23.4), with 67% of the generalization effect attributable to implicit transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 demonstrate that cross-modal generalization occurs largely through implicit mechanisms rather than explicit reasoning. The partial correlation analysis appropriately controls for explicit knowledge, and the strong statistical support (high Bayes factors) indicates robust implicit transfer. The quantification of implicit vs explicit contributions (67% implicit) is well-supported.

results.result: Participants demonstrated strong within-modality learning and zero-shot across-modality generalization that were highly correlated, enabling scene segmentation into objects based purely on statistical information without boundary cues. This learning produced genuinely coherent object-like representations consistent across visual and haptic modalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 and C58-C60 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. These are well-supported by the convergent evidence from within-modality learning (C23-C25, C38-C40), cross-modal generalization (C26-C33, C39-C47), within-participant consistency (C52-C53), and implicit transfer analyses (C54-C57).

results.result: The authors propose that statistical learning mechanisms revealed in adults might operate in infant cognitive development, based on infant studies using similar stimuli and the parsimony principle that infants possess similar sensitivity to co-occurrence statistics.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 and C71 extend findings to developmental implications. While the citations to infant literature are appropriate (C34-C35) and the parsimony argument is reasonable (C36), this remains speculative (C37, C71) as no infant data were collected in the current study. The proposal is plausible but requires empirical validation.

results.result: The results suggest that classical object identification criteria (cohesion, boundedness, rigidity, no action at a distance) may be sufficient but not necessary, potentially representing special cases of a more general principle of statistical coherence. However, statistically-defined representations may need to pass additional criteria to become full mental objects.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 propose theoretical reinterpretation of classical object criteria. While the current findings (C73-C74) challenge necessity of classical criteria, the proposal that they are special cases of statistical coherence (C75) is speculative. The acknowledgment that additional criteria may be needed (C76) appropriately recognizes limitations.

results.result: Previous statistical learning studies focused on single modalities or simultaneous multimodal presentation but did not test cross-modal generalization or investigate objectness of representations. The current findings suggest deeper integration where statistically-defined information in one modality automatically integrates into modality-general object representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C70 appropriately characterize prior work (C63-C69 with citations) and position the current contribution. The characterization of previous limitations is accurate, and the conclusion about deeper integration (C70) is supported by the cross-modal generalization and within-participant consistency findings.

results.result: While not providing direct mechanistic evidence, the results suggest participants developed compressed representations (latent chunks) during exposure that mediated cross-modal effects. This occurred without specialized learning cues and despite the large number of stimuli (444 scenes) that could not be retained in raw form.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C88 appropriately acknowledge the lack of direct mechanistic evidence (C81) while proposing plausible computational mechanisms based on prior work (C82, C86-C87). The inference about compressed representations (C84-C85) is reasonable given the stimulus complexity, and the proposal about latent chunks (C88) is consistent with cited theoretical frameworks.

results.result: Statistical learning is proposed to be not only domain-general but also to produce domain-general internal representations that could underlie affordances and object concept abstraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 synthesize the findings with appropriate citations. The domain-generality claim (C90) is supported by the cross-modal transfer findings. The proposal about affordances and object concepts (C91) is appropriately framed as speculative ('could be') while being grounded in the empirical results and relevant theoretical frameworks.

results.result: The study included 28 participants in the visual exposure experiment (8 excluded for failing haptic training, final N=20) and 20 participants in the haptic exposure experiment (none excluded). All protocols were ethically approved.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 describe participant samples and ethical approval. The exclusion criteria (C93) are clearly justified and applied consistently. The different exclusion rates between experiments (C93 vs C96) are explained by the different roles of haptic training in each design.

results.result: The experimental procedures involved specific numbers of trials and force levels: 444 unique visual scenes with each pair appearing 222 times; pulling forces of 7.5N (separating objects) and 22.5N (breaking objects) in visual exposure experiment; three force levels (7.5N, 15N, 22.5N) in haptic exposure experiment; 48 haptic pulling test trials and 72 visual familiarity trials in visual exposure experiment; 192 haptic exposure trials and 32 visual familiarity trials in haptic exposure experiment.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C126 provide detailed methodological specifications. These are clearly described and internally consistent. The different numbers of trials across experiments are appropriate given the different experimental designs and complexity of the tasks.

results.result: Participants showed discriminable pulling forces: 9.3±3.3N difference between force levels in visual exposure experiment; 5.4±1.2N difference between low-medium and 2.8±1.7N between medium-high levels in haptic exposure experiment.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 report manipulation checks showing participants could discriminate the force levels. The larger difference in the visual exposure experiment (C128) compared to haptic exposure (C129-C130) is consistent with the two-level vs three-level design. These data validate that the haptic task was performed appropriately.

results.result: The introduction establishes that objects are fundamental to cognition, defined by consistent sensory properties and affordances. While classic theories emphasize visual boundaries, these are insufficient alone. Statistical learning can segment inputs without boundary cues, but whether this produces real object-like representations was previously unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C16 provide appropriate background and motivation. The characterization of prior work is accurate with proper citations (C3, C8-C10, C12-C13, C15). The identification of the knowledge gap (C2, C14) appropriately motivates the current study. The definition of objects (C16) provides a clear operational criterion.

results.result: While implicit statistical learning over short periods is difficult and performance was not perfect, participants who learned well within one modality showed strong cross-modal generalization beyond what explicit knowledge would predict.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 appropriately contextualize the findings. The acknowledgment of imperfect performance (C61) with citation is honest, while the emphasis on individual differences and strong generalizers (C62) correctly identifies the key pattern in the data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that objectness may exist on a continuum and that further work is needed to refine necessary and sufficient conditions. Differences in behavioral measures (looking times vs cross-modal generalization) also require attention. The work represents an important first step connecting statistical learning to infant object representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 appropriately identify limitations and future directions. The acknowledgment of a continuum of objectness (C77) and need for further work (C78-C79) shows appropriate scientific caution. The characterization of the contribution (C80) is reasonable given the novel cross-modal generalization paradigm.
